https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Just Stop Oil pair deface Charles Darwin’s grave at Westminster Abbey
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Alyson Lee, 66, and Di Bligh, 77, have been arrested and say the naturalist would have approved
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Two Just Stop Oil activists have been arrested after they defaced Charles Darwin’s grave at Westminster Abbey with orange chalk.
Alyson Lee, 66, and Di Bligh, 77, covered the white marble gravestone with a message that said “1.5 is dead!” at about 10am on Monday. It was a reference to reports last week that average global temperatures in 2024 had for the first time exceeded 1.5C above the pre-industrial era.
“We have passed the 1.5-degree threshold that was supposed to keep us safe,” one of the activists said. “Darwin would be turning in his grave to know we are in the midst of the sixth mass extinction.”
The women sat next to the grave before they were led away from Westminster Abbey by the police.
Lee said: “We are trying to get the government to act on climate change. They are not doing enough.”
Bligh, a former chief executive of Reading council, added: “Darwin once said, ‘It is not the strongest of the species, nor the most intelligent that survives. It is the one that is the most adaptable to change, that lives within the means available and works co-operatively against common threats’.
“Last year was the hottest since modern humans evolved. If we do not work together to rein in the corporations and billionaires driving us beyond our means, humanity will not be able to adapt to what is coming.”
Lee said: “I believe he would approve because he was a good scientist and he would be following the science, and he would be as upset as us with the government for ignoring the science.”
Conservators are cleaning the memorial and the Abbey remains open.
A spokesman said they did not believe the orange chalk would cause any permanent damage, adding: “Westminster Abbey can confirm that orange chalk was sprayed by climate activists on Charles Darwin’s gravestone today.
“The Abbey’s conservators are taking immediate action to clean the memorial and do not anticipate that there will be any permanent damage. The police were called to the scene and dealt with the incident. The Abbey remains open for visiting and worshipping.”
Darwin, best known for his theory of evolution by natural selection, died in 1882. He is buried in Westminster Abbey’s scientists’ corner, along with Isaac Newton and Stephen Hawking.
Just Stop Oil activists have staged a number of high-profile protests in recent years, including by disrupting sports and theatre events, painting over the US embassy building in London and throwing soup at Van Gogh paintings.
A Metropolitan Police spokesman said: “Two women have been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage with what is believed to be powdered paint at Westminster Abbey. Police were called shortly after 10am on Monday, January 13, following reports that the women had been detained by security. They have been taken to a central London police station where they remain in custody.”

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Court ruling casts doubt on future of Rosebank oil field
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.subtitle: Verdict challenges the approval of big North Sea projects, citing insufficient consideration of emissions
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
A judge has quashed consent for two huge North Sea oil and gas projects in a ruling that campaigners claim casts doubt on the future of the industry.
Shell’s Jackdaw gas field and Equinor’s Rosebank oil field must now re-apply for government permission because their original approvals failed to consider the emissions that will be generated when the oil and gas are burnt.
Neither project will be able to start production unless consent is granted afresh but the companies have been allowed to continue development work in the meantime.
Wael Sawan, Shell’s chief executive, called on the government for urgent support to re-approve Jackdaw, which was originally granted consent in 2022 and is half built at a cost of about £800 million.
The gas field, about 155 miles east of Aberdeen, is due to start up in 2026 and provide enough gas to fuel 1.4 million homes. Sawan said it was a “critical piece of national infrastructure” to help Britain to avoid becoming more reliant on imports.
Rosebank, 80 miles northwest of Shetland, is owned by Equinor and Ithaca Energy. It is the largest untapped oil field in UK waters and was given consent in September 2023.
The campaign groups Greenpeace and Uplift brought the legal challenge appealing against the government’s decision to give consent to the Rosebank and Jackdaw projects.
A Supreme Court ruling last summer concluded that the impact assessments for new projects had to consider the effects of burning the oil and gas that is extracted from the fields.
• What the court ruling on North Sea oil and gas means for Scotland
The new verdict from Lord Ericht, at the Court of Session in Edinburgh, agreed that the initial approvals for Rosebank and Jackdaw were unlawful because they had not done so.
Shell and Equinor had argued that the consent for their projects should remain despite this but Ericht ruled against them. “The public interest in authorities acting lawfully and the private interest of members of the public in climate change outweigh the private interest of the developers,” he said.
Regulators must now reassess the projects in line with new guidance that the government is still finalising and is expected to publish this spring.
The fate of the fields will be a test of the government’s approach to the North Sea. Ed Miliband, the energy secretary, has vowed to stop issuing new North Sea oil and gas licences and described Rosebank as a “colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism” while in opposition.
However, both Rosebank and Jackdaw received their licences years ago; the case centres instead on development permits for projects within existing licence areas.
• Pragmatism must prevail over ideology when it comes to North Sea
A spokeswoman for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “The government has already consulted on revised environmental guidance to take into account emissions from burning extracted oil and gas to provide stability for industry, support investment, protect jobs and deliver economic growth.
“We will respond to this consultation as soon as possible and developers will be able to apply for consents under this revised regime. Our priority is to deliver a fair, orderly and prosperous transition in the North Sea in line with our climate and legal obligations, which drives towards our clean energy future of energy security, lower bills and good, long-term jobs.”
Analysts at Stifel, the investment bank, said they did not expect the assessment of emissions to result in the reversal of the previous decisions to approve the projects and believed the ruling would have “no impact”.
However, Gail Anderson, a research director at the energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie, said the ruling was likely to result in longer lead times to approve projects “which will not help UK supply and energy security”.
Sawan told The Times that the Ericht ruling was a “mixed verdict” and Shell was pleased that it had not been forced to halt work. He called for the government to provide “the appropriate signals that continue to give us the confidence to invest”.
He added: “We would really hope that the government now leans in and supports us in building what we continue to believe is a critical piece of national infrastructure.
“The chancellor is rightly talking about support for growth in the economy. The majority of growth is enabled by energy. In a world where today gas storage levels are at five-year lows, we have a project here that could potentially heat 1.4 million homes in the UK from domestic North Sea gas … rather than importing that gas. It’s a slam dunk for me and I really hope that we get the urgent support from the government to be able to now issue the license and allow us to move ahead.”
He said gas was “a core part of what the UK will need” in its future energy mix and he believed that there was “a very high likelihood that the government will see that and I’m hopeful will provide the right support for it rather than incentivising more imports”.
In June last year the UK Supreme Court ruled in favour of the campaigner Sarah Finch that Surrey county council’s approval of the Horse Hill onshore drilling project was unlawful as the “scope 3” emissions — those generated by the consumers of the energy products — had not been considered as part of the environmental impact assessment.
The judicial review of consent for Rosebank and Jackdaw was held in Edinburgh in November last year after Greenpeace and Uplift brought forward their cases.
Philip Evans, a senior campaigner at Greenpeace UK, described the verdict as a “historic win” for environmentalists.
He said: “The age of governments approving new drilling sites by ignoring their climate impacts is over. The courts have agreed with what climate campaigners have said all along: Rosebank and Jackdaw are unlawful and their full climate impacts must now be properly considered.
“Fossil fuels are an economic dead end. Now that the ball is back in the government’s court, ministers have the opportunity to sort out the legal mess left by their predecessors. They should use this moment to set out a new path for the North Sea, reaffirming their commitment to no new oil and gas and prioritising clean energy.”
Tessa Khan, the executive director of Uplift, said: “Rosebank is a bad deal for the UK. Most of its oil will be exported and sold on the international market, doing nothing to lower our energy bills or boost UK energy security.
“If Equinor and Ithaca Energy try to push Rosebank through despite this ruling, the government must reject it. To do otherwise would undermine its ambitious clean growth plans by sending a signal to investors that the UK isn’t serious about transitioning away from expensive oil and gas.”
Douglas Lumsden, the energy and net-zero spokesman for the Scottish Conservatives, said: “This decision is a hammer blow for the North Sea oil and gas industry, which is so crucial for our economy and energy security.”
Russell Borthwick, chief executive of Aberdeen & Grampian Chamber of Commerce, said: “Allowing work on Jackdaw and Rosebank to continue is a victory for common sense and averts what could have been an international embarrassment for the UK on energy security and investment.”
A Shell spokesman said: “Today’s ruling rightly allows work to progress on this nationally important energy project while new consents are sought. Swift action is needed from the government so that we and other North Sea operators can make decisions about vital UK energy infrastructure.
“When operational, Jackdaw would provide enough fuel to heat 1.4 million UK homes, at a time when older gas fields are reaching the end of their production and the UK is reliant on imported gas to meet its energy needs.”
Equinor said it was pleased with the ruling as it allowed Rosebank to move forward while awaiting new consents. It said Equinor and Ithaca had committed £2.2 billion towards developing the licence.
It added: “We welcome the court’s judgment, which enables Equinor to continue developing a project expected to create up to 2,000 UK jobs during its development phase.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Sadiq Khan vows to block Rachel Reeves’s Heathrow plans — as it happened
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Ed Miliband missed Rachel Reeves’s speech because he was “in meetings”, a source close to the energy secretary said.
The former Labour leader has been a vocal opponent of a third runway in the past and told MPs that expansion at Heathrow “won’t go ahead” unless it is in line with the UK’s net zero targets.
Other cabinet ministers with relevant briefs — including the business and transport secretaries — came to support Reeves but Miliband was not present, despite mentions in the chancellor’s speech of net zero and clean energy programmes.
Miliband, who voted against a third runway in 2018 “on grounds of both climate and air pollution”, was also absent for prime minister’s questions, in which Sir Keir Starmer defended his growth plans. Asked last week if he would resign over a new runway, Miliband said: “Don’t be ridiculous — no. The whole of the government is focused, and I’m focused, on delivering our clean energy mission.”
The third runway at Heathrow is a “dead cat” and the chancellor “hasn’t a clue” on how to deliver growth, the head of Ryanair has said.
Michael O’Leary, CEO of the Irish airline, said: “The UK continues to lose out on enormous growth opportunities because you have a chancellor who hasn’t a clue about how to deliver growth, has had five years to get ready for it, and yet has managed to screw it up in her first budget.
“The third runway at Heathrow is a dead cat. If it ever arrives, it will be about 2040, 2045 or 2050, in fact long after I’ve departed from Ryanair. It will not deliver any growth.”
Ryanair’s UK base is London Stansted airport. It does not fly from Heathrow.
Rachel Reeves’s announcement for another runway at Heathrow “is the most irresponsible announcement from any government since the Liz Truss budget”, the Green Party has said.
Siân Berry, the Green MP for Brighton Pavilion, said the plan to reach net zero by 2050 will be almost “impossible” if any new runway is built.
“The chancellor talked about the ‘costs of irresponsibility’, but expanding airports in the face of a climate emergency is the most irresponsible announcement from any government I have seen since the Liz Truss budget,” Berry said.
“The carbon cost of expanding Heathrow, Luton, and Gatwick together will cancel out the benefits of Labour’s keystone clean energy plan.”
Sir Sadiq Khan has said he and other opponents to a third runway at Heathrow will use “whatever means we can” to stop it going ahead.
The Labour mayor of London hinted he could use the courts to challenge the announcement as it makes progress.
Speaking to the BBC, Khan said: “When Heathrow comes out with their plans, as I’m sure they inevitably will, we will scrutinise them carefully. And we’ll have to hold the government to task about them supporting a plan that doesn’t address the three concerns I’ve set out.”
Asked if this challenge could take place in the courts, he added: “We will use whatever means we can.”
The new chief executive of easyJet has welcomed the expansion of Heathrow, saying it presents “a unique opportunity” for the low-cost carrier to operate from the airport in the future.
It already largely serves hub airports in continental Europe, including Charles de Gaulle in Paris, Schiphol in Amsterdam and Geneva, but has never had slots for Heathrow, where capacity is significantly constrained.
Kenton Jarvis said: “I welcome the government’s pro-growth agenda and their recognition of the importance of aviation and the crucial role it plays as an enabler of economic growth. As an island nation, this industry provides much-needed connectivity as well as creating many skilled jobs which contribute to the wider prosperity of the country.
“Expansion at Heathrow will provide consumer and economic benefits and represents a unique opportunity for easyJet to operate from the airport at scale for the first time and bring with it lower fares for consumers.”
The chancellor’s endorsement for airport expansion was widely condemned by environmentalists.
“Expanding airport capacity would wipe out all the benefits of the government’s clean power plan, and won’t provide any benefits for ordinary people,” said Adrian Ramsay, the Green party co-leader, referring to proposals by the energy secretary, Ed Miliband, to source 95 per cent of electricity from low carbon sources by 2030.
Doug Parr, Greenpeace’s policy director, said: “A third runway at Heathrow is unlikely to boost the UK economy but will certainly boot noise, air pollution and climate emissions.”
Green Alliance, a non-party political think tank, said the UK could not have growth at any cost. “The economic case for bigger airports and new roads is highly questionable, and it’s crystal clear that pushing ahead with these will fly in the face of the UK’s climate targets,” said Shaun Spiers, the group’s executive director.
Miliband told MPs this week that airport expansions “won’t go ahead” if they are incompatible with the UK’s carbon budgets, which currently run up to 2037.
Rachel Reeves “does not understand business”, the Conservative Party has said as it reiterated an attack on her budget.
Mel Stride, the shadow chancellor, said: “The biggest barriers to growth in this country are Rachel Reeves, Keir Starmer and their job-destroying budget — and nothing in the chancellor’s speech proved otherwise.
“What’s worse, the anti-growth chancellor could not rule out coming back with yet more tax rises in March.”
The Liberal Democrats said Reeves was refusing to pull the “single biggest lever” for economic growth: a closer relationship with the European Union.
“If this government was serious about boosting growth, it would start negotiating a new UK-EU trade deal with a bespoke customs union at its heart,” the party said.
Stephen Phipson, chief executive of Make UK, the country’s leading industrial and manufacturing trade body, said that industry would welcome the “upbeat, forceful and positive statement from the chancellor”.
He added that companies have become “very frustrated at the UK’s longstanding, sclerotic approach” to reforms in areas such as planning and infrastructure investment.
Nonetheless, he warned that the next 12 months were set to be “immensely challenging” thanks to the wider international environment and pointed to contradictions in Labour’s policies.
“There is a clear contradiction between implementing laudable measures such as planning reform and infrastructure investment whilst, at the same time, applying a handbrake through measures which will inevitably reduce investment and freeze recruitment,” Phipson said.
The boss of Heathrow airport has welcomed the “bold responsible vision” outlined by Rachel Reeves in her speech today.
Thomas Woldbye, the Heathrow CEO, said: “This is the bold, responsible vision the UK needs to thrive in the 21st century and I thank the government and chancellor for their leadership.
“It has given us the confidence to confirm our continued support for expanding Heathrow.
“Successfully delivering the project at pace requires policy change — particularly around necessary airspace modernisation and making the regulatory model fit for purpose.
“We will now work with the government on the expected planning reform and support ministers to deliver the changes which will set us on track to securing planning permission before the end of this parliament.”
The mayor of London said he “remains opposed” to a third runway, adding that he is “not convinced” that it will not be hugely damaging for the environment.
In a statement, Sir Sadiq Khan said: “I remain opposed to a new runway at Heathrow airport because of the severe impact it will have on noise, air pollution and meeting our climate change targets.”
He pledged to scrutinise any proposals, but did not mention any plan to legally challenge the decision.
“Despite the progress that’s been made in the aviation sector to make it more sustainable, I’m simply not convinced that you can have hundreds of thousands of additional flights at Heathrow every year without a hugely damaging impact on our environment,” he said
Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, the insurance group, said that businesses and the economy needed policies that would “stay the course”.
“Nothing kills economic confidence like a constantly changing landscape,” Blanc said.
She added that while the UK’s regulatory environment played a significant role in attracting foreign investment, the UK needed an approach which “balances the desire for safety in the system with the need for growth.”
She added: “If we can strike a better balance between the two, companies like Aviva can release the necessary capital to fund the vital infrastructure projects the country so desperately needs.
“But perhaps more importantly, it will allow millions of businesses to better plan for their future with a greater degree of certainty.”
Julia Pyke, the joint managing director at Sizewell C, said that Rachel Reeves’s focus on investment growth “highlights the urgent need for bold, future-proof infrastructure investment”.
According to EDF, which is developing Sizewell C alongside the UK government, the nuclear plant will start generating electricity in 2035 if it gets the go-ahead by the summer
“The UK must build smarter, investing in long-term solutions that drive prosperity and leave a legacy for future generations,” Pyke added.
Rachel Reeves has said that the government will reduce net migration even if it means less economic growth.
Asked about her plans by reporters, she said: “We will reduce net migration. But taking back control means having more say of who comes into this country.
“That’s why I announced in Davos last week that we’re looking at visa routes for some of the most highly skilled and talented people.”
She also said that she had no plans to publish her tax return: “Chancellors and prime ministers haven’t published their tax returns in the past, and I don’t have any plans to do so.”
Justin Sullivan, president of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, the independent regulator of Britain’s property industry, said that Reeves was “correcting the course of Labour’s growth journey”.
Sullivan said that the speech will help “reset the mood” after confidence among companies in the built environment tailed off following Labour’s budget.
While Reeves has focused on major projects such as the East West Rail link, Sullivan added that the Treasury needed to work with councils and other government departments to improve smaller-scale infrastructure projects such as local road networks, water utilities, and public transport links.
Analysis by Steven Swinford and Oliver Wright
Rachel Reeves’s speech on growth presented an inherent contradiction. Taken at face value the chancellor is evangelistic about the need to grow the economy. Economic growth, she said, should run through everything the government is doing. Ministers, she said, will have a fight on its hands but they are up for it.
There was a flurry of announcements to go with it. Backing a third runway at Heathrow. Relaxing planning constraints. Taking on the newts and bats. Building Britain’s very own Silicon Valley near Cambridge. Unlocking money from pension schemes.
The challenge for Reeves is that many of the growth measures she is advocating will take many years to come to fruition. A third runway at Heathrow is almost certainly a decade away and proposals for new Oxford and Cambridge arc of development, linked by new transport infrastructure, will likely take longer still.
• Read our analysis in full
The chancellor has said that the government supports a third runway at Heathrow as she added that the UK “cannot duck the decision any longer”.
She said that Heathrow was “at the heart of the UK’s openness as a country” and that UK growth has “been constrained” by not building it.
“We cannot duck the decision any longer,” she said. “I have always been clear that a third runway at Heathrow would unlock growth boost investment and increase exports and make the UK more open and connected, and now the case is stronger than ever.”
She invited proposals to be brought forward by the summer and added that any “associated surface transport costs” would be financed through private funding.
“Heathrow themselves are clear their proposals for expansion will make strict rules on noise, air quality and carbon emissions.”
The runway could make Britain “the world’s best connected place to do business”, she added. “Now is the time to grasp the huge opportunity in front of us.
“The prize on offer if we do this is immense the next generation with more opportunity than the last.”
Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said that Reeve’s speech aimed to reset the narrative around growth after the October budget which was widely criticised for being “anti-business”.
Her speech today also set out a series of policies and initiatives aimed at improving the UK’s growth prospects.
However, Dales said: “The key point that is often missed is that, rather than taking place in isolation, these must be introduced as part of a programme of measures that encompasses everything from savings and investment to the labour market and public services.”
Siemens Healthineers, the company that hosted Rachel Reeves’ speech, is itself investing £250 million to build a state-of-the-art superconducting magnet manufacturing facility in Bicester, Oxfordshire.
The new facility is set to open in 2026 and will pioneer groundbreaking MRI scanning technology. It is expected to host more than 1,000 skilled jobs.
Ghada Trotabas, managing director of Siemens Healthineers Great Britain & Ireland, said that the investment “underscores our long-term commitment to investing in innovation and supporting the government’s plans to build a strong, thriving economy.”
The chancellor has said that she and the government are “not satisfied” with the state of the UK economy.
“There is still more we can and will do,” she said. “I am not satisfied with the position we are in. While we have huge amounts of potential the structural problems in our economy run deep.
“This has to be our focus for the duration of the parliament because the situation demands us to do more.”
She spoke about making it easier to build homes around train stations and a host of transport connections in the north that she would like to improve.
She also backed plans to create a “Wembley of the north” at Old Trafford, which she said “promises to create new housing and commercial development around a new stadium.”
Rachel Reeves said that she has been “genuinely shocked” about how slow the UK’s planning system is and wants developers to focus on building rather than “worrying about bats and newts”.
Speaking in Oxfordshire, the chancellor said: “I have been genuinely shocked about how slow our planning system is about how long it takes to get things done.
Speaking about the slow delivery of a solar farm in Cambridgeshire. “It’s ridiculous, the deputy PM has already driven significant progress across government on these issues.
“The problems in our economy, the lack of bold reform we have seen over decades can be summed by the £100 million bat tunnel built for HS2, the type of decision that has made building major infrastructure in our economy far too expensive and far too slow.”
She said that developers will now be able to pay into a nature restoration funds, “so they can focus on getting things built and stop worrying about the bats and the newts.”
The chancellor has defended her much-criticised budget, saying there are “costs to responsibility”.
In her speech, Reeves said: “At my first budget in October it was my duty as chancellor to fix the foundations of our economy and repair the public finances we inherited.
“I protected working people after a cost of living crisis by freezing fuel duty and not increasing income tax, national insurance and VAT.
“The increase in employers’ NI contributions has consequences on business and beyond, I accept that there are costs to responsibility, but the costs of irresponsibility will be far greater. Those who oppose my budget know that too.”
She said that her approach to economic growth will be based on stability, reform and investment.
Rachel Reeves has said that the government has “begun to turn things around” in the economy after years of high inflation and the cost of living crisis.
Speaking at a Siemens Healthineers magnet facility in Oxfordshire, the chancellor said that “economic growth is the number one mission of this government” and helps to fund more police, reduce waiting times and put more money in people’s pockets.
“For too long we have accepted low expectations and accepted decline — we no longer have to do that,” she said.
In the audience were a host of cabinet ministers including Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary.
Although the government will today signal its backing for a third runway at Heathrow Airport, many steps still remain before any building can start.
The airport will need to submit a planning application to the government but, even with that approval, this could be held up by the courts over concerns about air quality, noise or the government’s net zero commitments.
Moreover, the plan for the new runway is complex and would involve demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers and re-routing the M25 — the UK’s busiest motorway — through a tunnel.
In 2014, it was projected to cost £14 billion but with the increasing cost of labour and building materials it would now be expected to significantly exceed this.
Rachel Reeves will not “shy away” from the fact that some of the government’s choices have been difficult for business, Jonathan Reynolds said.
The business secretary said: “The chancellor will be candid in her speech and recognised we have had to ask things of business to repair the national finances. We do not shy away from that.
“If being responsible was easy, other governments would have done it.”
• Rachel Reeves: Britain needs a dose of Trump positivity
The business secretary suggested it would take less than a decade to build a third runway at Heathrow and said the country “can’t afford” for such projects not to go ahead.
Jonathan Reynolds said that he did not recognise a timetable of ten years to build a third runway, but suggested planning changes would mean it would not take that long.
He told BBC Breakfast: “It’s not just about aviation expansion, there’s a whole range of things.”
He added: “We simply cannot afford to say we don’t build reservoirs any more, we don’t build railways, we don’t build runways. That’s not good enough, we will be left behind.”
People will feel the impact of the government’s growth policies “this year” as changes will unleash Britain’s “animal spirits”, the business secretary has said.
Jonathan Reynolds told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “I think people will feel the difference in their pockets this year because inflation is coming down, wages are rising, and the kind of, I believe, excitement, dynamism we will generate in the UK from showing people we are willing to make these decisions to tackle these difficult issues, that unleashes the animal spirit, the sense of something exciting is happening.”
• What are Labour’s plans to boost growth? The key economic policies
In a preview of her speech today, Rachel Reeves said that she hoped her plan to create an Oxford-Cambridge growth corridor would turn the area into “Europe’s Silicon Valley”.
She said that the 66-mile growth corridor going from the UK’s most well-known university cities — via Milton Keynes — would become the “home of British innovation”.
The plan includes a railway to connect two new reservoirs to improve water infrastructure, new laboratory space and 4,500 new homes.
Lord Patrick Vallance, the government’s chief scientific officer during the pandemic, has been appointed as the scheme’s champion.
He said that it would help the area “build on its existing strengths in academia, life sciences, semiconductors, AI and green technology”.
Growth is the defining mission of this government (Sir Keir Starmer writes). It is the only way to deliver our Plan for Change and put more money in people’s pockets. The only cure for the sickness of stagnation and decline.
We should be confident about Britain’s prospects. Inflation is falling. Wages are growing at their fastest rate for three years. More than 70,000 jobs have been created since July. The UK was voted the second most attractive destination for private investment. We are on track to be the fastest-growing major economy in Europe — that is what leading agencies like the International Monetary Fund predict.
But as the chancellor will set out in her speech today, we can go further and faster. Because there is a morass of regulation that effectively bans billions of pounds more of investment from flowing into Britain. Thickets of red tape that, for all the Tories talked a good game, was allowed to spread through the British economy like Japanese knotweed. Our pledge today is that this government will do what they could not. We will kick down the barriers to building, clear out the regulatory weeds and allow a new era of British growth to bloom.
• Labour’s policies will usher in a ‘big build’ era, the prime minister writes
A Labour donor has criticised Rachel Reeves’s plan to build a new runway at Heathrow, saying it would be an “illusion of growth”.
Dale Vince, who owns the green energy company Ecotricity, said the decision was a “mistake” and will mean the UK does not effectively cut its carbon emissions.
The multimillionaire, who donated more than £5 million to Labour before the last election, told the BBC: “It’ll take ten years to build a runway, cost maybe £50 billion. It’ll create the wrong kind of growth — we’ll be exporting tourism money abroad, creating a bigger imbalance than we already have, and it will come at the expense of our carbon-cutting effort.
“I think it’s the wrong kind of growth … We’ve got to decarbonise energy, transport and food, and at the moment we’re on course to do energy, and we won’t do that with this Heathrow expansion, which is a big mistake.”
The government will not fund any of the “sporting elements” of the Old Trafford stadium redevelopment, the business secretary has said.
In her speech today Rachel Reeves is set to announce plans to build a “Wembley of the north”, regenerating the area around the Manchester United stadium with housing and infrastructure.
The plans also include a new 100,000-seater stadium for the club, which is owned by the billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe. He has been criticised for attempting to have taxpayer-funded investment increase the value of his club.
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said Ratcliffe would have to pay for the stadium himself.
“We are not funding any of the sporting elements of that, but of course the wider area, transport, housing,” he said.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/arts/article.title: Gold rush for Glastonbury despite Neil Young’s cancellation
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/arts/article.subtitle: The Canadian star pulls out of the 2025 festival lineup in protest at the ‘corporate’ BBC presence, but a land purchase hints at healthy finances
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/arts/article.text:
Neil Young may not be bringing his Harvest to “corporate” Glastonbury but the festival seems set on further expansion after reporting record profits.
Young, 79, withdrew from this year’s festival on Tuesday, but the organisers revealed a doubling of profits in their annual accounts and hinted at expansion of the 900-acre site at Worthy Farm in Somerset, having spent £3.65 million on a new land.
Last year, the festival, which hosted 4,000 performances on more than 100 stages, drew 210,000 people over its five days. Tickets for this year’s event, which cost nearly £380, sold out in 35 minutes.
• Neil Young returns to Spotify two years after vaccine row
Young, one of the world’s most acclaimed musicians with a career spanning six decades, said he was pulling out of Glastonbury because it was a “corporate turn-off” and blamed the BBC, the holder of its broadcasting rights since 1997.
In a post on his website, Young said he and his band, the Chrome Hearts, had been looking forward to the festival, which he described as “one of my all time favourite outdoor gigs”.
But Young added: “We were told that the BBC was now a partner in Glastonbury and wanted us to do a lot of things in a way we were not interested in. It seems Glastonbury is now under corporate controls and is not the way I remember it being.”
He said: “We will not be playing Glastonbury on this tour because it is a corporate turn-off, and not for me like it used to be.”
While the festival has plenty of corporate partnerships, including with Vodafone and Co-op, it is the BBC’s presence that is felt largest. It deploys more than 50km of fibre optic cable to connect 65 cameras on five stages. In 2023 it broadcast 90 hours of performances and its coverage was watched by 23 million people.
• Divas, drones and downpours: Backstage with the BBC at Glastonbury
Young, who came to fame in the 1960s and 1970s with albums such as After the Gold Rush and Harvest, had not yet been announced for this year’s Glastonbury.
He clashed with the BBC when he headlined the festival in 2009. Following complaints by viewers about the corporation’s brief coverage of Young’s set that year, it said that after two months of discussions, the singer had allowed them to show only five songs.
“Neil Young’s career has been conducted on his own terms,” Mark Cooper, the BBC’s head of music television at the time, said, adding that Young’s management “agreed to let TV and radio broadcast five songs as they watched and listened to his performance”.
“They believe in the live event and retaining its mystery and that of their artist,” Cooper added.
Young’s withdrawal leaves a headline-sized hole in this year’s programme, with only Rod Stewart confirmed.
Last year’s headliners were Dua Lipa, Coldplay and SZA, with Shania Twain in the Sunday afternoon legends slot.
• 17 best Glastonbury performances of all time
The festival, which did not respond to requests for comment, appears to be in rude financial health.
Its accounts show that turnover in the year to March 2024 grew by £11 million to £68 million, with pre-tax profits doubling to nearly £6 million. It donated more than £5 million to organisations including the NHS and Greenpeace and gave more than £1 million to local groups and charities in return for services such as volunteer stewards.
They also show that Sir Michael Eavis, 89, the dairy farmer who founded the festival in 1970, has transferred his shares to his daughter, Emily, who already runs “day-to-day organisation”.
In a previous statement to the Financial Times, the festival said: “Following record losses caused by Covid — when Glastonbury’s 2020 and 2021 events were unable to go ahead, costing the festival millions — we were pleased to enjoy successful, dry Glastonburys in both 2023 and 2024.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Labour donor Dale Vince says £43.5m divorce bill is total vindication
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: The Ecotricity founder accused his ex-wife Kate of bringing an ‘abusive’ case and said he had originally offered her £12 million more
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
A green energy industrialist has accused his ex-wife of running an “abusive” divorce case after she was awarded more than £40 million following their separation.
Dale Vince, a former donor to Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion who is estimated to be worth £100 million, has been in a four-year dispute with Kate Vince over how their money should be split.
Mr Justice Cusworth said on Friday that the Labour donor could pay his ex-wife in three tranches, of £13.94 million, £14.49 million and £15.08 million, including interest, totalling £43.51 million.
The 63-year-old founder of Britain’s first green energy supplier, Ecotricity, said the judgment was “a total vindication” after he claimed the amount awarded was £12 million less than he initially offered.
• Inside Dale Vince’s messy divorce
Ms Vince’s lawyers told the court that her ex-husband was giving away their matrimonial assets, of which she should be entitled to half, including £5,460,000 in donations to the Labour Party between April 2022 and May 2024.
Mr Vince, who also runs the vegan, carbon-neutral football club Forest Green Rovers, claimed the increase in donations and other spending came from a rise in the value of his business, alleging it had “nothing at all to do with” their legal battle.
The first payment is due to be made by April 30, with the remaining two to follow each year.
Speaking after the judgment, he said: “Today is a total vindication of my approach to this case from the very beginning. My ex-wife walks away from court with £12 million less than I first offered her four years ago. Along with her legal team she has wasted years of time, not just our own — that of the court, and some £6 million in fees.”
Ms Vince, 50, had told the High Court last year that her ex-husband had “no problem in participating in conspicuous consumerism”, adding that he flew in private jets, drove powerful petrol-powered cars and owned a 56ft luxury yacht. Under cross-examination, he denied her claims, including that they had shared a romantic helicopter ride over a Canadian glacier on their wedding day in February 2006.
A barrister representing Ms Vince told a High Court judge last October that her estranged husband was convinced that he was in line for a peerage from Sir Keir Starmer’s government, and that he was attempting to hasten their divorce so she would not benefit from his potential elevation to the House of Lords.
She denied that she was using the hearings to humiliate her ex-husband. Her lawyer told the court that it was a “great pity” that her husband “has adopted this course and thereby exposed sensitive matters such as the chance of him obtaining the reward of an honour to public gaze”.
A lawyer representing Mr Vince said the claim was an attempt to turn the hearing into a “circus”.
In 2016 his first wife, Kathleen Wyatt, who he married in 1981 and divorced 11 years later, was awarded £300,000 by a judge. She began legal action in 2011 seeking £1.9 million and the businessman spent more than £500,000 fighting the case. He said at the time: “I think it is very wrong just to cash in what is in effect a very old lottery ticket on her part.”
It emerged during the pre-trial proceedings that Dale and Kate Vince met in 1997, when she was one of two graduate employees at his Renewable Energy Company, which eventually evolved into Ecotricity Limited.
Mr Vince, who has donated more than £5 million to Labour, making him one of the party’s leading funders, previously told the High Court he did not want to sell “his life’s work” to pay for his divorce settlement.
He said that the final judgment demonstrated how “such reckless, abusive cases, so lacking in legal merit, should not be allowed”.
Sarah Jane Lenihan, a partner at Dawson Cornwell, representing Kate Vince, said: “We are very grateful to the court for the fair and equitable award granted to Ms Vince.
“It is only right that Ms Vince has received an award which reflects her extensive contributions throughout the marriage, which the judge acknowledged, during which Mr Vince built the majority of his fortune.”
